title: Shared Trajectories in Soil Microbial Succession Across Five Glacier Forefields in the Arctic and Antarctica
content:
Across five polar glacier forefields with significantly different species pools, we found that process- and trait-based trajectories of microbial succession were broadly conserved. Succession was characterized by increasing richness, decelerating rates of change, increasing spatial variation among sites and between soil depths, and parallel shifts from fast- to slow-growing taxa and from autotrophs to heterotrophs.


ABSTRACT

Glacial retreat exposes new forefield soils for microbial colonization and succession, which shape early soil development and biogeochemical functioning. However, key dimensions of succession—including variation across microbial domains, abundant and rare subcommunities, and soil depths—remain poorly resolved, constraining the ability to predict postglacial successional trajectories and their functional consequences. Here, we integrate measures of taxonomic diversity, phylogenetic structure, and colonist life history traits derived from rRNA metabarcoding data to characterize bacterial and microeukaryotic succession in surface and deep soils across five glacier forefields in the Canadian High Arctic and Antarctic Peninsula. Despite substantial differences in local species pools, process- and trait-based successional trajectories were broadly conserved among forefields. Microbial abundance and taxonomic richness increased over time, rates of community change decelerated as soil conditions stabilized, and turnover was consistently dominated by species replacement. Trait-based indices further indicated a shift from fast-growing, spatially widespread taxa towards slower-growing, more spatially restricted lineages, paralleling a transition from autotroph- to heterotroph-dominated communities. Contrary to canonical expectations of deterministic community convergence, spatial variation among sites and between soil depths increased through time, an effect that was strongly context-dependent: abundant bacterial taxa converged in membership, whereas microeukaryotes and rare taxa were more strongly shaped by stochastic processes, producing patchier, site-specific assemblages. Together, our results indicate that microbial succession in polar forefields follows conserved, trait-mediated trajectories despite underlying taxonomic variability, but diverges from alpine systems in the persistence of spatial heterogeneity and stochasticity. Process- and trait-based approaches may therefore provide more robust predictions of soil development and biogeochemical feedbacks in expanding ice-free landscapes.
